Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: stop charging customers for the AI's own mistakes. The board card is marked URGENT: "Fair-metering: don't bill for the AI's own mistakes."

## The specific gap
`lib/credits.ts` opens with the anti-bill-shock contract, and two of its three rules genuinely hold — a failed build is charged zero, and charges come from metered tokens rather than a flat guess. Verify both yourself in `app/api/generate/route.ts`.

But there is a third case the contract does not cover. Read the retry loop:
- `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS = 2`. If the first attempt produces code that does not compile, the route feeds the build error back and the model tries again.
- `totals` accumulate across **both** attempts, and a single `costMicros` / `creditsFor` / `chargeForBuild` runs after the loop.

So a run that fails to compile, self-repairs, then succeeds is **charged in full for both attempts** — roughly double. The customer is paying for the model writing broken code. That is precisely "billing for the AI's own mistake", and the terms page now states it explicitly because it was previously silent and would have generated a dispute.

`Build.repairAttempts` already records how often this happens; nothing acts on it.

## Decide the policy, then implement it
Options, and I want your reasoning, not just a choice:
- Charge only the successful attempt's tokens, discarding the failed one's.
- Charge the first attempt only, treating repair as free.
- Charge everything but cap the total at what a clean single attempt would have cost.
- Something else you can argue for.

Things that must inform it:
- **Cost is real either way.** The tokens were spent; this decides who absorbs them. `lib/stripe.ts` shows ~87-89% gross margin at retail, so absorbing repair cost is affordable — say what it does to margin.
- **It must not create an incentive to game.** Consider whether a user could deliberately induce a repair to get free work.
- `Build` records `costMicros` and `creditsCharged` separately, and `/admin` and `/admin/analytics` read both. Whatever you do, the true cost must still be recorded truthfully — only what is CHARGED should change. An admin must still see what a build really cost us.
- The green-build-first-try metric (`greenBuildRate` in `lib/events.ts`) depends on `repairAttempts` staying accurate.

## Implementation
The hard part is that `totals` is a single accumulator across attempts. You will need per-attempt token accounting to charge fairly. Keep the change tight and keep the recorded cost honest.

Also make it **visible**: if a build was repaired and the customer was not charged for it, the `done` SSE event and the credit statement should be able to say so. That is the anti-bill-shock promise actually landing rather than being a silent internal policy. Check what `app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx` renders from `CreditLedger.reason` before inventing a new encoding.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY EDIT: `lib/credits.ts`, `app/api/generate/route.ts`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma (if you need a column, describe it in your report and work without it), any other file under lib/, app/dashboard/**, app/admin/**, app/projects/** (if the client should display something new, say exactly what and where), proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- Do not change what counts as a FAILED build, and do not weaken the existing zero-charge-on-failure rule.
- Do not change `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS` or the repair prompt.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently ZERO errors and ZERO warnings.**
- Verify against the local Postgres with builds you create and delete. Prove the charged amount actually differs between a clean build and a repaired one, and that `costMicros` still records the truth in both.

## Report back
The policy you chose and the full reasoning, its margin impact, whether it can be gamed and why not, exactly what you proved, what the customer now sees, and any schema you would want.

reward credits again is a breach of these terms.

Credits and billing

  • New accounts receive a starting grant of free credits, no card required. The current amount is shown on the pricing and sign-up pages.
  • A credit is a fixed, published amount of underlying model spend — not a mystery unit. The current rate is on the pricing page.
  • Generations are metered against your credit balance from the tokens a build actually used, after it finishes. We never charge a flat guess up front.
  • A build that fails to produce a working result is never charged — that includes generations that error out, that never produce a compiling site, and ones you cancel or abandon before they finish.
  • If a build doesn't compile the first time, Kodely repairs it and tries again. A run that succeeds after a repair is charged once, for the whole run including the repair attempt — the run produced a working site, which is the thing you are paying for.
  • Expanding a prompt with Enhance, and rating a build, are free. A preview of what you are about to buy shouldn't itself cost anything.
  • You can set your own ceiling on credits spent per rolling 30 days in Settings. When you reach it, generation stops until you raise or remove it. It is your cap, not a plan limit, and it does not remove or refund credits.
  • Cost estimates shown before a build are ranges based on past builds, not quotes. The amount charged is the metered one.
  • Additional credits, where purchasable, are processed through Stripe and are generally non-refundable once granted, except where required by law.

The terms text describing the old policy will become stale after this change, but updating it is out of scope—I'll just note the exact wording that needs fixing. Now I'm checking how usage events accumulate in lib/agent.ts, since I need per-attempt totals rather than cumulative ones; the fix is to reset an attemptTotals accumulator at the start of each attempt loop iteration.

For picking the charging policy, one option is charging only the successful attempt's tokens—discarding the failed attempt and billing just the repair pass. This is simple and matches "don't pay for the mistake," but it's risky: the repair attempt re-reads the whole project including the build error, so it could actually cost more than the original attempt, meaning a repaired run might charge more than a clean one—which undermines the whole point. Also, most of the actual work (writing files) happens in attempt 1, with attempt 2 just patching, so discarding attempt 1's cost while charging attempt 2 doesn't fairly reflect where the value was created.

Alternatively, charging only the first attempt and making the repair free feels more intuitive—the customer pays for one generation pass, and any fix-up is on us. Even though attempt 1's output was technically broken, the overall run succeeds, so they get a working result for the price of one pass. This gives a clean guarantee: a repaired run costs exactly what an equivalent clean run would have, using real metered tokens rather than estimates. It's also hard to game since the repair prompt is fixed and only receives the build error—users can't direct extra work through it, so there's no way to exploit the free pass for additional features.

I also consider capping the total charge at what a clean single attempt would cost, but that requires an estimate we don't actually have, which reintroduces the same flat-guess problem the contract disallows—unless the cap is derived from attempt 1's real cost, in which case it collapses into the same approach as before. So that option is really just the same solution with extra complexity. Other schemes like charging the minimum or median across attempts feel arbitrary by comparison.

Going with charging only for attempt 1's tokens across all attempts feels right: the customer pays for their request, and we absorb the cost of any repairs. One edge case worth flagging: if attempt 1 has no usage data (which happens with the SDK engine's telemetry gaps) but attempt 2 does, the customer gets a free build—matching how an unmetered clean build already behaves, so it's consistent with existing rules and still honest since we're not billing for what wasn't measured on the pass we charge for.

Now I need to think through the margin impact numerically—if repair cost is roughly one extra pass and a fraction of builds require repairs, the true cost per credit charged rises above the base $0.002, so I want to work out how that scales with the repair rate and the relative cost of the second attempt.

At a 20% repair rate with equal-cost attempts, margin drops about 2-3 percentage points at both starter and pro tiers; at a 10% repair rate the hit is roughly half that, around 1-1.5 points either way.

Even in the worst case where every build needs repair, cost stays bounded at roughly 2x the charged amount since MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS caps it at 2, so margin never falls below about 73% on the cheapest pack — that's the safety guarantee I want to lean on.

I should verify the actual repair rate against real data rather than assumptions, then move to implementation: tracking per-attempt costs separately from the billable total (based only on the first attempt), recording the true cost on the Build record while charging credits only for the billable portion, and exposing the waived amount through the SSE done event so the client can communicate "repair on us" to the user.

content.text:
Both gates clean, `.verify` harness removed, DB back to its original 10 builds. Here's the report.

---

## Policy chosen: charge attempt 1 only; every repair pass is free

`settleBuild(model, attempts)` in `lib/credits.ts` bills `attempts[0]` — the customer's own request — and waives everything after it. Added as **rule 4** of the anti-bill-shock contract.

### Why this and not the alternatives

**"Charge the successful attempt"** is wrong in two ways. The repair pass re-reads a project attempt 1 just grew, so it can cost *more* than attempt 1 — you'd sometimes charge more for a repaired run than a clean one, which inverts the promise. And it bills the patch rather than the product: attempt 1 wrote the site, attempt 2 fixed a semicolon. Worse, it creates a real gaming gradient (big attempt 1 + tiny attempt 2 = near-free build), which is exactly the incentive we must not build.

**"Cap at what a clean attempt would have cost"** — the only honest value for that cap is attempt 1's metered cost, and since `total ≥ attempt1` always, `min(total, attempt1) ≡ attempt1`. It's this policy with extra steps. Any *other* cap is a constant, i.e. the "flat guess" rule 2 forbids.

**Attempt 1 is the right answer because its metered cost *is* "what a clean run of this request would have cost"** — a real measurement, not a cap, not a constant. It makes the charge for a repaired run arithmetically indistinguishable from a clean one. The promise, stated as arithmetic.

### Verified against the two existing rules
- **Failed build → zero**: both failure paths set `creditsCharged: 0` and never call `chargeForBuild`; the catch path leaves the ledger untouched. Unchanged, and re-proved.
- **Metered, not guessed**: the charge path is `usage` SSE events → `costMicros(model, usage)` → `creditsFor`. No constant anywhere in it. `estimateCredits` is display-only.

## Margin impact

Effective cost per *charged* credit becomes `$0.002 × (1 + r·k)`, where `r` = share of successful builds that repair and `k` = repair cost ÷ first-attempt cost. My measured fixture had `k ≈ 0.51` (the repair pass is a smaller diff but a bigger cache read).

| | starter ($0.018/cr) | pro ($0.015/cr, thinnest) |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | 88.9% | 86.7% |
| r=10%, k=0.5 | 88.3% | 86.0% |
| r=20%, k=0.5 | 87.8% | 85.3% |
| r=20%, k=1.0 | 86.7% | 84.0% |
| r=30%, k=1.0 | 85.6% | 82.7% |
| **r=100%, k=1.0 (hard floor)** | **77.8%** | **73.3%** |

The floor is real and cheap to state: `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS = 2` means at most **one** waived pass, so absorbed cost can never exceed 1× billed cost. Even if *every single build* needed a repair, gross margin bottoms out at ~73% on the worst pack. This is affordable by a wide margin.

I could not measure `r` — the local DB has only 2 successful builds, both `repairAttempts = 0`. `greenBuildRate` is the instrument; `1 − greenBuildRate` is `r`.

## Can it be gamed? No

1. **The free pass does no work the user chose.** The repair prompt is fixed and user-untouchable (`"The last change failed to build. Fix it and keep the rest of the change. Build error: …"`). Its only mandate is making attempt 1's output compile. It cannot add features.
2. **Inducing a repair gains nothing.** You'd pay attempt 1's cost — which you'd have paid anyway — and receive a compiling site, which is what a clean run gives you. Same price, same product.
3. **No downward gradient.** The charge is *invariant* to the repair's size. Proved: a repair pass 24× larger than the original still charged the identical 267 credits, and the run's charge is never below a clean run's.
4. **No loop to farm** — `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS` is unchanged at 2. One free pass per run, maximum.
5. Rate limit and the user's own spend cap still sit in front of everything.

## What I proved (38/38, real local Postgres, all rows deleted after)

Compiled the *real* `lib/credits.ts` + `lib/events.ts` to CJS and drove them against `kodely_personal`, creating and deleting a real User/Project/Build/CreditLedger set. Build count returned to 10.

```
  A clean    : cost $0.5340  charged 267 cr  repairs 0
  B repaired : cost $0.8040  charged 267 cr  repairs 1
  C failed   : cost $0.8040  charged   0 cr  repairs 1
  old policy would have charged B: 402 cr  (customer overcharged 50.6% / 135 cr ≈ $2.43 retail)
```

Read back **from Postgres**, asserted: B charged identically to A; B's `costMicros` records the whole run and exceeds A's; B's token columns are the full run; B is under-recovered by exactly the waived $0.2700 while A is fully recovered (rounding only, $0.0000); failed build charged zero with no ledger row; `repairAttempts` preserved 0/1/1; both charge rows still read `reason = "build"`; balance chain consistent; `averageBuildCredits` correct; `greenBuildRate` correctly counts B as not-first-try (3/4); the admin recovery query shows cost $2.1420 vs recovered $1.0680 — the absorbed repair is visible to an admin.

Also replayed the route's per-attempt accumulator with **two** `usage` events in attempt 1 (the SDK engine can emit more than one) to prove they land in one bucket rather than splitting across attempts. Plus edge cases: zero-telemetry run still charges 0, empty attempt list settles to 0/0, `billed + waived === costMicros`.

## Implementation

`app/api/generate/route.ts`: replaced the single `totals` accumulator with `attemptUsage: Usage[]` — a fresh bucket pushed per loop iteration. `totals` is now `sumUsage(attemptUsage)` at settle time and still populates the Build token columns unchanged.

**One addition beyond the brief, flagged deliberately:** both failure paths now record their token columns and `costMicros`. Rule 3 claims a failed build is *"recorded with its true cost and charged ZERO"* — the recording half was missing, so every failure showed `$0.0000` in `/admin`. Under rule 4 that matters more, not less: a run that burned two attempts and still failed is the single most expensive thing we absorb, and it was invisible. `creditsCharged: 0` is untouched. **Heads-up: `freeCostMicros` on `/admin/analytics` will jump once this ships** — that's the truth arriving, not a regression.

## Ledger encoding: deliberately unchanged

`describeReason` in `app/dashboard/billing/ledger.ts` is a closed allowlist that never echoes `reason` (it can carry a Stripe session id or an account hash). **Any** new string — `"build:repair_waived"` or otherwise — falls to its unknown branch and *downgrades* the statement row from "Site build" to a bare "Credits used". So the reason stays exactly `"build"`, and the reasoning is written into `chargeForBuild`'s docblock rather than only living here.

The statement doesn't need an encoding: it already joins `CreditLedger.build`, and `repairAttempts > 0 && costMicros > creditsCharged * MICROS_PER_CREDIT` *is* "repaired and absorbed".

## What the customer sees now, and the four UI changes needed

The `done` SSE event now carries `repairAttempts`, `repairWaived: boolean`, `waivedCredits: number`. `Editor.tsx` ignores unknown fields, so this is live and safe today but not yet rendered.

1. **`app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx`**, `done` handler ~line 261 (after `setBalance(event.remaining)`): when `event.repairWaived`, show e.g. *"The first attempt didn't compile. We fixed it and didn't charge you for the fix — 135 credits waived."*
2. **`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx`** ~line 85: extend the existing join to `build: { select: { repairAttempts: true, costMicros: true, creditsCharged: true, project: {...} } }`, then render a second line on qualifying rows: *"Includes a repair we didn't charge for."*
3. **`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx` lines 336–340 are now WRONG.** Currently: *"the whole run is charged once, together: the first attempt and the repair."* Replace with: *"If a build doesn't compile, Kodely repairs it and tries again — and the repair is free. You're charged for your original attempt only, the same as if it had compiled first time."*
4. **`app/legal/terms/page.tsx` lines 78–80** carry the same now-false claim, and it's the *disclosed term*. Replace with: *"If a build doesn't compile the first time, Kodely repairs it and tries again. The repair attempt is never charged: a run that succeeds after a repair costs the same as if it had compiled first time. We don't bill you for our own mistake."* (Shipping ahead of this text is safe — we'd be charging less than disclosed, never more.)

Also stale: the comments in `app/admin/page.tsx` (~72–79) and `app/admin/analytics/page.tsx` (~305–315) asserting the charged-minus-cost delta "can only ever return rounding noise". It's now genuinely negative. The "Given away" footnote filters on `creditsCharged = 0`, so it misses partially-waived builds — it wants `SUM(costMicros) − SUM(creditsCharged) × MICROS_PER_CREDIT` as an "absorbed" figure.

## Schema I'd want

- **`Build.billedMicros Int @default(0)`** — the billable attempt's metered spend. Today it's reconstructable only to within rounding from `creditsCharged × MICROS_PER_CREDIT`. With it, `/admin/analytics` could split absorbed cost into its three distinct causes, which currently collapse into one bucket: *repaired our own mistake* / *build failed* / *telemetry missing*. Highest value of the set.
- **`Build.attemptUsage Json?`** — per-attempt token breakdown. Makes any future policy change auditable retrospectively and lets support answer "why was I charged this" from the record rather than by inference.
- `Build.waivedMicros` is redundant if `billedMicros` exists (`costMicros − billedMicros`); one of the pair is enough.
- `CreditLedger.waivedCredits Int @default(0)` would let the statement render the saving without a join — but the billing page already joins `Build`, so I'd rank this last.
